overview: Simon de Montfort was a younger son of a French crusading house who claimed an English earldom, married the king's sister, and ended by governing England through a council while its king was his prisoner. He led the movement that imposed the Provisions of Oxford on Henry III of England in 1258, destroyed the royal army at the Battle of Lewes in May 1264, and summoned the parliament of January 1265 that called knights of the shire and burgesses together for the first time.

He was killed at the Battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265 and his body cut apart on the field.

birth.note: The year is not recorded exactly; about 1208 is the usual estimate, and he was the third surviving son of Simon de Montfort the elder and Alix de Montmorency.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Simon de Montfort was a younger son of a French crusading house who claimed an English earldom, married the king's sister, and ended by governing England through a council while its king was his prisoner. He led the movement that imposed the Provisions of Oxford on Henry III of England in 1258, destroyed the royal army at the Battle of Lewes in May 1264, and summoned the parliament of January 1265 that called knights of the shire and burgesses to Westminster together for the first time.

He was never king and never claimed to be. Every writ of his fifteen months in power ran in Henry's name, which was both the source of his authority and the thing that made the regime impossible to defend once the magnates who had made it began to leave it. Killed at the Battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265, he was mourned as a martyr in the Midlands and denounced as a traitor at court, and he has been argued over on those two terms ever since.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: He was born about 1208 at Montfort-l'Amaury, west of Paris, the third surviving son of Simon de Montfort the elder and Alix de Montmorency. His father commanded the Albigensian Crusade in Languedoc and was killed at the siege of Toulouse in 1218 by a stone from a mangonel, leaving a reputation for ferocious effectiveness and very little for a third son. The English claim came through his grandmother Amicia, sister of the last Beaumont earl of Leicester, and in 1229 Simon agreed with his elder brother Amaury to divide the inheritance: Amaury kept the French lands, Simon took the English claim and crossed to England in 1230 with, as he later recalled, no English.

Henry III gave him the honour of Leicester in 1231 and invested him formally as earl in February 1239, nearly a decade later. One of his first acts as lord of Leicester was to expel the town's Jewish community, in a charter granting that no Jew should dwell there in his time or the time of any of his heirs to the end of the world; he gave the lands they had held to the nuns of St Mary de Pratis and described the act as good for his soul. It was not an aberration of his later career but the first fixed point in it, and the debts owed to Jewish lenders would be a war aim of his supporters thirty years later.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: The friendliest evidence comes from churchmen who knew him. Robert Grosseteste, bishop of Lincoln, and the Oxford Franciscan Adam Marsh were his correspondents and Marsh was his spiritual director; from their letters it is clear that Montfort had read and taken to heart Grosseteste's tract distinguishing a king from a tyrant, which is as close as the record comes to showing where his political language was learned. The same letters are not flattery. Marsh writes to him about his impatience and the harshness of his temper, and urges restraint on a man who evidently needed to be urged - a friend's warning rather than an enemy's charge, which is what makes it worth having.

The hostile view was formed in Gascony and finished at court. The lords and townsmen he governed between 1248 and 1252 accused him of ruling by seizure and imprisonment; royalist opinion after 1258 added the charge that a Frenchman by birth had made himself master of England and gaoler of its king, and the men who killed him at Evesham dismembered the body in a way that was meant to say exactly that. Matthew Paris and Adam Marsh, the two chroniclers closest to him, were both sympathisers, so the surviving picture is drawn largely by partisans on one side or the other, and the middle ground has to be reconstructed from what he actually did.

What the Midlands made of him is a third source in its own right. Within months of his death the monks of Evesham were recording miracles at his grave, the reform party's songs were circulating, and a man excommunicated in life was being venerated as a martyr. Modern historians read him more coolly without dismissing him: John Maddicott's portrait - zealous, intelligent, uncompromising, and convinced of his own rectitude - also traces the reforming commitment back to private grievance, above all his recall from Gascony and his wife's unsettled claims against the crown, and finds public principle and family advantage so entangled in 1264 and 1265 that no account separating them cleanly is likely to be true.

contentSections.title: The king's sister, and the king's enmity
paragraphs: In January 1238 Montfort married Eleanor, Henry III's youngest sister and the widow of William Marshal the younger. The marriage was made privately in the king's chapel at Westminster with Henry's consent but without consulting the magnates, and it was a scandal twice over: Eleanor had taken a vow of perpetual chastity before the archbishop of Canterbury after her first husband's death, and a great royal marriage disposed of in secret was exactly the kind of decision the baronage expected to be consulted on. Richard of Cornwall, the king's brother, went into armed opposition and was bought off; Montfort went to Rome and obtained a dispensation.

The favour did not last. At the queen's churching in August 1239 Henry turned on him publicly, called him excommunicate, accused him of seducing Eleanor before the marriage and of naming the king as surety for his debts without leave, and drove him out of the country. They were reconciled repeatedly over the next twenty years and the underlying quarrel never closed, partly because Eleanor's dower from the Marshal estates was never properly settled and the couple pressed the claim for decades. Montfort went on the Barons' Crusade of 1240 to 1242, where the barons of the Kingdom of Jerusalem thought well enough of him to ask him to govern them, and came home to serve in Henry's failed Poitevin campaign of 1242, whose mismanagement he did not trouble to hide his opinion of.

contentSections.title: Gascony, 1248-1252
paragraphs: In 1248 Henry appointed him the king's lieutenant in Gascony for seven years, with orders to pacify a duchy that had become ungovernable. He did it by force: he broke the feuding factions of Bordeaux, took castles, imprisoned opponents, and made war on Gaston de Bearn and the lords of the south. The duchy quietened and the complaints multiplied, and in 1252 the Gascons brought them to Westminster - oppression, arbitrary imprisonment, seizures - and Henry put his own lieutenant on trial before the magnates.

The trial is the hinge of his life. The magnates heard the charges and effectively cleared him; Henry, unconvinced, disputed his accounts and disowned him anyway, and Montfort resigned the lieutenancy and withdrew to France, where after the death of Blanche of Castile he was sounded out about a place in the French regency. He was reconciled and back in Henry's service by 1253. But he had been publicly abandoned by a king he had served at his own expense, and every later account of him - his own, his friends', and the modern scholarship - treats that grievance as the beginning of the politics that ended at Evesham.

contentSections.title: The Provisions of Oxford and the road to war
paragraphs: The crisis of 1258 was made by money. Henry had accepted the crown of Sicily from the pope for his second son Edmund and with it a debt the English church and kingdom were expected to pay, while the king's Poitevin half-brothers monopolised patronage and a famine year sharpened everything. At the Oxford parliament of June 1258 a group of magnates came armed and imposed the Provisions of Oxford: a council of fifteen chosen jointly, parliaments three times a year, a justiciar answerable for the shires, and reforming inquests into local government. Montfort was one of the seven who swore the original confederation, and he became the man least willing to let any of it lapse.

The Provisions of Westminster of October 1259 extended the reform downwards, restricting the private courts and exactions of the great lords themselves. Montfort supported them, and in doing so lost much of the baronial support the movement depended on - the Earl of Gloucester and others had wanted the king restrained, not themselves. The alliance thinned from that point: a reform party of knights, townsmen and reforming clergy around Montfort, and a magnate class increasingly willing to live with the king.

In 1261 Henry obtained papal absolution from his oath and resumed personal rule; Montfort left for France in disgust. He returned in April 1263 at the invitation of barons who had decided the king would never keep terms, and the country slid towards war. Both sides then submitted the quarrel to Louis IX of France, who gave judgment at Amiens on 23 January 1264 and annulled the Provisions outright. The Mise of Amiens left no lawful road to reform at all. Fighting began within weeks, royal forces stormed Northampton in April and took Montfort's son Simon the Younger prisoner, and on 14 May 1264 Montfort came down off the downs above Lewes.

contentSections.title: The government of England, 1264-1265
paragraphs: The Battle of Lewes gave him the king, the king's brother Richard of Cornwall and the king's heir the Lord Edward, all in one afternoon. The Mise of Lewes agreed that night left Henry his crown and took his government: a council of nine ruled in his name, chosen under Montfort's influence, with Edward and Henry of Almain held as hostages for the settlement. For fifteen months Montfort was the effective ruler of England without holding any office that said so, which is the central oddity of his regime and the reason its enemies could call everything he did unlawful.

The base narrowed steadily. His sons took castles, prisoners and ransoms on a scale that looked to contemporaries like a family helping itself, and Gilbert de Clare, Earl of Gloucester - who had commanded the baronial centre at Lewes - fell out with him over precisely that and went over to the royalists in the spring of 1265. To hold the west Montfort made a treaty with Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in June 1265 that recognised him as Prince of Wales in exchange for money and troops, terms no English government negotiating from strength would have conceded. The papal legate Ottobuono, refused entry to the kingdom, excommunicated the regime from Boulogne.

On 28 May 1265 the Lord Edward escaped from loose custody at Hereford and joined Gloucester and Roger Mortimer in the Marches. Edward took Gloucester town on 29 June, closing the Severn crossings and pinning Montfort in south Wales, and on the night of 1 August surprised the younger Simon's army outside Kenilworth and captured its banners. Montfort forded the Severn at Kempsey on 2 August to join a son whose force had already been broken, and halted at Evesham on the evening of 3 August.

contentSections.title: The parliament of January 1265
paragraphs: The writs went out in December 1264 for an assembly at Westminster on 20 January 1265, and it sat until the middle of March. Its shape is the reason it is remembered: 23 lay barons, about 120 churchmen, two knights from every shire as had been tried in 1264, and - for the first time in England - two burgesses from each of a list of boroughs, among them York, Lincoln, Sandwich and the Cinque Ports. Its business was the enforcement of the Provisions of Westminster, judicial relief for men squeezed by lords, and the terms on which the Lord Edward might be released.

It was not the first House of Commons, and calling it that obscures what actually happened. There was no separate chamber, no continuous institution, nothing resembling a general election, and no claim that the men summoned represented anyone in a constitutional sense; the boroughs were chosen, not enumerated, and the assembly was summoned by a government looking for support in the two places it still had any. The 23 barons are the proof: Montfort called so few because so few would come. Jeffrey Hamilton's description - a very partisan assembly rather than a proto-democratic representative body - is the fair one.

What it did establish was a precedent about who could be summoned, and the precedent outlived the regime that set it. Edward I, who destroyed Montfort at Evesham, called knights and burgesses to his own parliaments in 1275 and again to the assembly of November 1295 later nicknamed the Model Parliament, and by the middle of the fourteenth century the knights and burgesses were sitting apart from the lords as a matter of course. Montfort did not design an institution. He needed the shires and the towns in January 1265, summoned them, and in doing so showed a king what could be done with them.

contentSections.title: Death at Evesham
paragraphs: On the morning of 4 August 1265 Edward came down on Evesham from the north with three divisions and blocked the neck of the loop of the Avon in which the town sits, with Mortimer's men holding the bridge behind. He advanced under the banners taken from the younger Simon two nights before, so that Montfort's watchman in the abbey tower first reported friends. Montfort, who had brought the captive Henry III onto the field in armour, attacked rather than waited, driving a wedge of knights at the royal centre in the hope of breaking out northwards.

The wedge stopped and the ring closed. His eldest son Henry de Montfort was killed early; the chronicle tradition gives the earl a set-piece on hearing it - that it was then time to die - and another commending their souls to God since their bodies were the enemy's, both written after the fact and both fitting the day. A squad of about a dozen men had been detailed to find him and kill him rather than take him, which is the clearest single indication that this was meant as an execution; one strand of the tradition has Roger Mortimer put a lance through his neck.

What followed was deliberate and public. The head, hands, feet and genitals were struck from the body, and the head was sent to Wigmore Castle as a present for Mortimer's wife, Maud. Hugh Despenser the justiciar and Peter de Montfort died in the same encirclement; his son Guy was badly wounded and captured; Henry III, wounded in the press while wearing Montfort's colours, was rescued only after shouting who he was. The drawing in British Library Cotton MS Nero D II, made within a generation, shows the dismembered body plainly enough that no later account had to invent the details.

contentSections.title: Legacy: the cult and the argument
paragraphs: The monks of Evesham gathered the trunk and buried it before the high altar, and within months people were reporting cures at the grave and at a spring by the battlefield. The abbey's miracle book recorded some two hundred of them, songs and laments for Earl Simon circulated in Latin, French and English, and a man who had died excommunicate was being treated as a martyr across the Midlands. The crown took it seriously enough to legislate: the Dictum of Kenilworth of 31 October 1266, the document that let the disinherited rebels buy their lands back, also asked the legate to forbid anyone to hold Simon holy or just and to silence the vain and foolish miracles attributed to him, under threat of punishment. The veneration went underground and continued to about 1280.

His reputation has swung with the politics of whoever was writing. Victorian constitutional history made him the father of representative government - Reinhold Pauli's biography of 1876 was subtitled the creator of the House of Commons - and that reading survives in the bas-relief of him among the lawgivers in the chamber of the United States House of Representatives. Twentieth-century scholarship dismantled it: the 1265 parliament was a manoeuvre by a narrowing regime, the council of nine was a vehicle for one family, and the reformer had begun as a courtier with a grievance about Gascony and a dowager sister-in-law's unpaid claims.

Neither reading survives on its own, which is why the argument is still worth having. The grievances were real and so was the programme: he kept the Provisions of Westminster when abandoning them would have bought him the magnates, and he was the only great man of his generation willing to be ruined for a constitutional principle - while also taking castles for his sons and conceding Wales to keep his army. The same is true of the darkest part of the record: the expulsion from Leicester in 1231, the cancellation of Jewish debts as a war aim, and the massacres carried out by his supporters at London, where a chronicle estimate puts the dead at about 500, and at Worcester, Canterbury and elsewhere. Leicester, whose clock tower still carries his statue, issued a formal rebuke of his antisemitism in 2001. The reform movement that first summoned England's towns to a parliament produced that too, and an account of him that leaves either half out is not an account of him.
